flashcards.q: What do RED and USE each stand for, and what is the key difference in what they apply to?
flashcards.a: RED = Rate, Errors, Duration -- for request-driven services. USE = Utilization, Saturation, Errors -- for finite resource pools (CPU, memory, disk, connection pools). Different subjects, not interchangeable.

flashcards.q: What are Google's four golden signals?
flashcards.a: Latency, traffic, errors, saturation -- effectively RED (latency=duration, traffic=rate, errors=errors) plus saturation borrowed from USE.

flashcards.q: How much downtime does a 99.9% monthly SLO allow, and how is it calculated?
flashcards.a: 43.2 minutes/month. 30 days = 43,200 minutes; 0.1% of that is 43.2 minutes.

flashcards.q: List the allowed monthly downtime for SLOs of 99%, 99.9%, 99.95%, and 99.99%.
What does an error-budget policy actually do, mechanically?
flashcards.a: When the error budget for the current rolling window is exhausted, feature releases freeze and the team shifts to reliability work until the budget recovers -- this is what connects an SLO to an actual release-cadence decision.

flashcards.q: Give a concrete cardinality-explosion example in Prometheus.
flashcards.a: A classic histogram with 10 buckets tracked across 50 services is already 500 time series before any additional label (region, version, endpoint) is added; each additional label with K unique values multiplies total series by K.

flashcards.q: What are native histograms in Prometheus, when did they stabilize, and what problem do they fix?
flashcards.a: Stable since Prometheus v3.8.0 (maturing through v3.13.0 LTS, 1 Jul 2026). They store an entire distribution in one sparse series with dynamic exponential bucketing instead of N separate bucket series, fixing the histogram-specific cardinality multiplication. Still opt-in via scrape_native_histograms, not default.

flashcards.q: What does a Prometheus recording rule do, and why use one?
flashcards.a: Precomputes an expensive or frequently-queried PromQL expression on a schedule and stores it as its own time series, so dashboards/alerts query the cheap precomputed series instead of recomputing an expensive aggregation live on every load.

flashcards.q: Why should alerts be symptom-based rather than cause-based?
flashcards.a: A cause-level metric (CPU, memory) can be elevated with no user impact (autoscaling working as designed), and users can be impacted by causes that never cross any infra threshold. Symptom-based alerts (the SLO itself burning) correlate directly with what users actually experience.

flashcards.q: Write the burn-rate formula and explain what a burn rate of 14.4x means.
flashcards.a: burn_rate = SLI_error_rate / (1 - SLO). A burn rate of 14.4x means that, sustained, you'd exhaust a full 30-day error budget in about 1 hour.

flashcards.q: What is multi-window multi-burn-rate (MWMBR) alerting, and what's the standard window-size guideline?
flashcards.a: An alert requires BOTH a short window (confirms the issue is current) and a long window (confirms it's sustained) to breach simultaneously before paging. Standard guideline: short window is about 1/12 the length of the long window.

flashcards.q: State the Google SRE Workbook's three burn-rate alert tiers with their windows and budget consumption.
flashcards.a: Page at 14.4x on 5m/1h windows (2% of 30-day budget in 1h). Page at 6x on 30m/6h windows (5% of budget in 6h). Ticket (not page) at 3x on 2h/24h windows (10% of budget in 24h).

flashcards.q: What is alert fatigue, and what is its observable symptom?
flashcards.a: Too many or too noisy alerts get muted/ignored by on-call, so the next real incident pages into silence. Symptom: a growing list of permanently-silenced alert rules, rising acknowledgment time, on-call self-reporting they ignore most pages.

flashcards.q: What is the concrete fix for alert fatigue?
flashcards.a: Track pages/week per on-call rotation as a first-class metric to actively reduce; require every alert to carry an actionable next step (a runbook link); delete alerts that fail that bar rather than endlessly re-tuning their thresholds.

flashcards.q: What Grafana feature, current as of version 13 (2026), addresses the problem of two teams' dashboards silently disagreeing about an incident?
flashcards.a: Dashboards-as-code: Git-backed dashboards edited through a PR workflow, so SLI/SLO definitions become version-controlled, reviewable artifacts instead of tribal knowledge embedded separately in each team's click-ops panel config.
